name: Chapter 5: Magnetism and Matter
description: Bar magnet, field lines, dipole in B, Gauss’s law for magnetism, M, H, χ, dia-, para- and ferromagnetism

cards.term: Origin of the word “magnet”, per NCERT?
cards.definition: From Magnesia in Greece, where magnetic ore was found as early as 600 BC

cards.term: Correction: NCERT calls Magnesia “an island”. Is it?
cards.definition: No: Magnesia is a region of Thessaly on the Greek mainland (there was also a city Magnesia in Asia Minor). Exams only ask “Magnesia”

cards.term: Earth’s magnetic field points roughly which way?
cards.definition: From geographic south to north (so Earth’s magnetic S pole is near the geographic North)

cards.term: Which end of a freely suspended bar magnet is its north pole?
cards.definition: The end that points to the geographic north

cards.term: Force between like and unlike magnetic poles?
cards.definition: Like poles repel, unlike poles attract

cards.term: A bar magnet is broken in two. What do you get?
cards.definition: Two smaller magnets, each with N and S poles and weaker properties — poles cannot be isolated

cards.term: What are magnetic monopoles? Do they exist?
cards.definition: Isolated N or S poles; not known to exist (unlike isolated electric charges)

cards.term: What does the iron-filing pattern around a bar magnet suggest?
cards.definition: The magnet is a magnetic dipole — two poles, like + and − of an electric dipole. A current-carrying solenoid gives the same pattern

cards.term: Compare the field lines of a bar magnet, a finite solenoid and an electric dipole.
cards.definition: Far away they look almost identical. Inside, the magnet’s and solenoid’s lines run S → N (closing the loops); the electric dipole’s run + → − (opposite)

cards.text: Magnetic field lines form {{c1::continuous closed loops}}; electric field lines {{c2::start on + charges and end on − charges (or at infinity)}}.

cards.term: What does the tangent to a magnetic field line give?
cards.definition: The direction of the net B at that point

cards.term: What does the density of field lines tell you?
cards.definition: Magnitude of B: more lines per unit area (normal to them) → stronger field

cards.term: Why can’t two magnetic field lines intersect?
cards.definition: At the crossing the field would have two directions — B must be unique

cards.term: How can you plot field lines without iron filings?
cards.definition: Move a small compass needle around and note its orientation at each point

cards.term: Why does NCERT avoid the term “magnetic lines of force”?
cards.definition: The force on a moving charge is perpendicular to B (qv × B), not along the line — so the lines do not show the direction of force

cards.term: Why can a bar magnet be treated as an equivalent solenoid?
cards.definition: Same field-line pattern; by Ampere’s hypothesis a magnet is a large number of circulating currents. Cutting either gives two weaker ones

cards.term: Far axial field of a solenoid (or bar magnet) of moment m?
cards.definition: \( B = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{2m}{r^3} \) (r ≫ size)

cards.term: Magnetic moment of a bar magnet equals…?
cards.definition: The moment of the equivalent solenoid that produces the same field (NIA)

cards.term: Torque on a magnetic dipole in a uniform B?
cards.definition: \( \vec\tau = \vec m\times\vec B,\quad \tau = mB\sin\theta \) (restoring)

cards.term: Net force on a magnetic dipole in a uniform B?
cards.definition: Zero — equal and opposite forces on the two poles; only a torque

cards.term: Potential energy of a magnetic dipole in B? Where is its zero?
cards.definition: \( U_m = -\vec m\cdot\vec B = -mB\cos\theta \); zero at θ = 90° (m ⊥ B)

cards.term: Minimum and maximum potential energy of a dipole in B?
cards.definition: Minimum −mB at θ = 0° (most stable); maximum +mB at θ = 180° (most unstable)

cards.term: Work needed to turn a dipole from θ₁ to θ₂ in B?
cards.definition: \( W = mB(\cos\theta_1 - \cos\theta_2) \); from 0° to 180° it is 2mB

cards.term: Teacher addition: period of small oscillations of a needle (moment of inertia 𝐼) in B?
cards.definition: \( T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{I}{mB}} \) — the Fig. 5.3(b) set-up; measure T to find B or m

cards.term: Intuition: why does a compass needle oscillate before settling?
cards.definition: Displaced from θ = 0, τ = −mB sin θ ≈ −mBθ acts like a spring → SHM about the field direction, damped by friction

cards.term: Example 5.1(a): a bar magnet is cut (i) across its length, (ii) along its length. Result?
cards.definition: Either way, two magnets, each with a N and S pole

cards.term: Example 5.1(b): a needle in a uniform B feels only a torque, but an iron nail near a magnet is attracted. Why?
cards.definition: The magnet’s field is non-uniform. The nail gets an induced moment; its induced S pole is nearer the magnet’s N pole, so net attraction

cards.term: Example 5.1(c): must every magnetic configuration have N and S poles?
cards.definition: No: only if it has a net non-zero moment. A toroid or a straight infinite wire has no poles

cards.term: Example 5.1(d): two identical iron bars, one surely a magnet. How to tell which, using only the bars?
cards.definition: Lower an end of A onto the end and then the middle of B. If the pull vanishes at B’s middle, B is the magnet; if no change, A is. (Repulsion anywhere → both magnetised)

cards.term: Replacements that turn electric dipole results into bar-magnet results?
cards.definition: \( \vec E\to\vec B,\ \vec p\to\vec m,\ \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\to\dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi} \)

cards.term: Equatorial field of a short bar magnet (r ≫ l)?
cards.definition: \( \vec B_E = -\dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{\vec m}{r^3} \) — opposite to m

cards.term: Axial field of a short bar magnet (r ≫ l)?
cards.definition: \( \vec B_A = \dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{2\vec m}{r^3} \) — along m; twice the equatorial value at the same r

cards.term: Table 5.1 · The dipole analogy
cards.definition: 1/ε₀: μ₀; Dipole moment p: m; Equatorial field −p/4πε₀r³: −μ₀m/4πr³; Axial field 2p/4πε₀r³: μ₀2m/4πr³; Torque p × E: m × B; Energy −p·E: −m·B

cards.term: Example 5.2: needle P at O (moment up); identical needle Q at positions Q₁–Q₆. Which are not in equilibrium?
cards.definition: PQ₁ and PQ₂: on P’s equator the field is downward, but Q points sideways → torque

cards.term: Example 5.2: which configurations are stable and which unstable?
cards.definition: Stable (Q ∥ B_P): PQ₃, PQ₆. Unstable (Q antiparallel): PQ₅, PQ₄

cards.term: Example 5.2: which configuration has the lowest potential energy? Why?
cards.definition: PQ₆: Q is along the field and on P’s axis, where B is twice the equatorial value at the same distance

cards.term: Trick for Example 5.2 type questions?
cards.definition: Find the direction of P’s field at Q (axis: along m_P; equator: opposite). Q ∥ B → stable, antiparallel → unstable, at an angle → not in equilibrium

cards.term: State Gauss’s law for magnetism.
cards.definition: The net magnetic flux through any closed surface is zero: \( \oint \vec B\cdot d\vec S = 0 \)

cards.term: Gauss’s law: electrostatics vs magnetism?
cards.definition: Electric flux = q/ε₀ (charges are sources and sinks). Magnetic flux = 0 — no monopoles, no sources or sinks of B

cards.term: Magnetic flux through a small area ΔS? Unit?
cards.definition: \( \Delta\phi_B = \vec B\cdot\Delta\vec S \); weber (Wb = T m²)

cards.term: Simplest magnetic element, according to Gauss’s law?
cards.definition: A dipole or current loop — all magnetism can be built from these

cards.term: Why is the magnetic flux zero through the Gaussian surfaces i and ii around a bar magnet?
cards.definition: Field lines are closed loops: every line that leaves also enters the surface, even around a pole

cards.term: Example 5.3(a): are these magnetic field lines right?
cards.definition: Wrong: lines can’t spring from a point (net flux ≠ 0). This is the electric field of a charged wire; B around a wire is circles

cards.term: Example 5.3(b): are these magnetic field lines right?
cards.definition: Wrong: lines cross, and a static B line can’t loop around empty space — a closed B loop must enclose a current

cards.term: Example 5.3(c): field lines of a toroid. Right?
cards.definition: Right: confined inside the toroid; each loop encloses current

cards.term: Example 5.3(d): straight, confined lines through a solenoid. Right?
cards.definition: Wrong: at the ends the lines must curve out and close; perfectly straight lines violate Ampere’s law

cards.term: Example 5.3(e): lines outside and inside a bar magnet. Right?
cards.definition: Right: inside they run S → N; the net flux around each pole is zero

cards.term: Example 5.3(f): lines pouring out of a plate. Magnetic?
cards.definition: Wrong for B (net flux out of the plate ≠ 0). It is the electric field of a + upper and − lower plate

cards.term: Example 5.3(g): perfectly straight lines between two pole pieces. Right?
cards.definition: Wrong: some fringing at the edges is inevitable (true for E between plates too)

cards.term: Example 5.4(a): are magnetic field lines lines of force on a moving charge?
cards.definition: No: the force qv × B is always normal to B

cards.term: Example 5.4(b): Gauss’s law for magnetism if monopoles existed?
cards.definition: \( \oint \vec B\cdot d\vec S = \mu_0 q_m \), q_m = enclosed magnetic charge

cards.term: Example 5.4(c): does a magnet exert a torque on itself? Does one element of a wire push another element of the same wire?
cards.definition: No self-force or self-torque on an element from its own field. But one element does act on another element of the same wire (zero for a straight wire)

cards.term: Example 5.4(d): can a system with zero net charge have a magnetic moment?
cards.definition: Yes: e.g. atoms of paramagnetic materials — neutral, but with net current loops

cards.term: Define magnetisation M. Unit and dimensions?
cards.definition: \( \vec M = \dfrac{\vec m_{net}}{V} \) (net moment per unit volume); A m⁻¹, [L⁻¹A]

cards.term: Field inside a solenoid filled with a magnetised core?
cards.definition: \( B = B_0 + B_m = \mu_0 nI + \mu_0 M \) — the core adds B_m = μ₀M

cards.term: Define magnetic intensity H. Unit?
cards.definition: \( \vec H = \dfrac{\vec B}{\mu_0} - \vec M \); A m⁻¹ (same as M)

cards.term: Total B in terms of H and M?
cards.definition: \( \vec B = \mu_0(\vec H + \vec M) \)

cards.term: What do H and M separately represent?
cards.definition: H: the part due to external causes (e.g. solenoid current, H = nI). M: the part due to the material itself

cards.term: Define magnetic susceptibility χ.
cards.definition: \( \chi = \dfrac{M}{H} \) — dimensionless; how strongly a material responds to H

cards.term: Sign of χ for para- and diamagnets?
cards.definition: Paramagnetic: small, positive. Diamagnetic: small, negative (M opposite to H)

cards.text: Relative permeability: {{c1::μᵣ = 1 + χ}}; permeability: {{c2::μ = μ₀μᵣ = μ₀(1 + χ)}}, so {{c3::B = μH}}.

cards.term: μᵣ is the magnetic analogue of what?
cards.definition: The dielectric constant K in electrostatics

cards.term: Of χ, μᵣ and μ, how many are independent?
cards.definition: One: given any one, the other two follow

cards.term: Solenoid with a magnetic core (Example 5.5)

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Example 5.5 · cored solenoid

Find the missing step.

Solenoid, n = 1000 turns/m, I = 2 A, core μᵣ = 400. Find H, B, M and the magnetising current I_M.
  1. H = nI = 1000 × 2 = 2 × 10³ A/m (independent of the core)
  2. B = μᵣμ₀H = 400 × 4π × 10⁻⁷ × 2 × 10³ ≈ 1.0 T
  3. ?
  4. Without the core: B = μ₀n(I + I_M) → 2 + I_M = 1/(4π × 10⁻⁴) ≈ 796 → I_M ≈ 794 A
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Example 5.5 · cored solenoid

Find the missing step.

Solenoid, n = 1000 turns/m, I = 2 A, core μᵣ = 400. Find H, B, M and the magnetising current I_M.
  1. H = nI = 1000 × 2 = 2 × 10³ A/m (independent of the core)
  2. B = μᵣμ₀H = 400 × 4π × 10⁻⁷ × 2 × 10³ ≈ 1.0 T
  3. M = (μᵣ − 1)H = 399 × 2 × 10³ ≈ 8 × 10⁵ A/m
  4. Without the core: B = μ₀n(I + I_M) → 2 + I_M = 1/(4π × 10⁻⁴) ≈ 796 → I_M ≈ 794 A

cards.term: What is the magnetising current I_M?
cards.definition: The extra current the windings would need, without the core, to produce the same B as with the core

cards.term: Correction: NCERT Example 5.5 has three slips. What are they?
cards.definition: (1) “H is dependent of the material” should read independent. (2) The parts (b), (c) solve B then M, swapping the question’s order. (3) I_M uses B = μᵣn(I + I_M); it must be μ₀n(I + I_M) — only that gives 794 A

cards.term: Classify materials by χ.
cards.definition: Diamagnetic: χ negative. Paramagnetic: χ small positive. Ferromagnetic: χ large positive

cards.term: Table 5.2 · χ and μᵣ by class
cards.definition: Diamagnetic χ: −1 ≤ χ < 0; Diamagnetic μᵣ: 0 ≤ μᵣ < 1  (μ < μ₀); Paramagnetic χ: 0 < χ < ε (small); Paramagnetic μᵣ: 1  μ₀); Ferromagnetic χ: χ ≫ 1; Ferromagnetic μᵣ: μᵣ ≫ 1  (μ ≫ μ₀)

cards.term: What are diamagnetic substances?
cards.definition: Substances that tend to move from stronger to weaker parts of a field — they are repelled by a magnet

cards.term: Field lines through a diamagnetic and a paramagnetic bar?
cards.definition: Diamagnetic (a): lines are expelled, field inside slightly reduced. Paramagnetic (b): lines concentrate, field inside slightly enhanced (about 1 part in 10⁵)

cards.term: Explain diamagnetism.
cards.definition: Atoms have zero net moment. An applied field slows electrons whose orbital moment is along B and speeds up those opposite (Lenz’s law), giving a net moment opposite to B → repulsion

cards.text: Diamagnetic examples: {{c1::bismuth, copper, lead, silicon, nitrogen (at STP), water and sodium chloride}}.

cards.term: Mnemonic: diamagnetic examples?
cards.definition: “Bright Copper Leads Silly New Workers to Salt” — Bi, Cu, Pb, Si, N₂, water, NaCl

cards.term: Is diamagnetism found in all substances?
cards.definition: Yes, it is universal — but so weak that para- or ferromagnetism masks it

cards.term: What is the Meissner effect?
cards.definition: Perfect diamagnetism of a superconductor: field lines are completely expelled; χ = −1, μᵣ = 0

cards.term: Two properties of superconductors?
cards.definition: Perfect conductivity and perfect diamagnetism, at very low temperatures

cards.term: Application of superconducting magnets named by NCERT?
cards.definition: Magnetically levitated superfast trains (maglev)

cards.term: Which theory explains superconductivity? When, and when was the Nobel prize?
cards.definition: BCS theory (Bardeen, Cooper, Schrieffer), 1957; NCERT dates its Nobel Prize to 1970

cards.term: Correction: NCERT says the BCS Nobel Prize came in 1970. Right year?
cards.definition: 1972 (Nobel Prize in Physics to Bardeen, Cooper and Schrieffer)

cards.term: What are paramagnetic substances?
cards.definition: Substances weakly magnetised in an external field; they move from weak to strong field — weakly attracted

cards.term: Explain paramagnetism.
cards.definition: Atoms have permanent dipole moments, randomised by thermal motion (no net M). A strong field at low temperature aligns them along B₀

cards.text: Paramagnetic examples: {{c1::aluminium, sodium, calcium, oxygen (at STP) and copper chloride}}.

cards.term: Mnemonic: paramagnetic examples?
cards.definition: “All Naughty Cats Often Chew Chillies” — Al, Na, Ca, O₂, CuCl₂

cards.term: How does a paramagnet’s magnetisation change with field and temperature?
cards.definition: Increases with stronger field and lower temperature, until saturation (all dipoles aligned)

cards.term: Teacher addition: Curie’s law?
cards.definition: \( \chi = \dfrac{C\mu_0}{T} \) — paramagnetic susceptibility ∝ 1/T (dia- and ferromagnetic χ don’t follow this)

cards.term: Oxygen vs nitrogen at STP: magnetic nature?
cards.definition: O₂ paramagnetic; N₂ diamagnetic (liquid O₂ sticks between magnet poles; liquid N₂ doesn’t)

cards.term: Water and copper: magnetic nature? Copper chloride?
cards.definition: Water and Cu: diamagnetic. CuCl₂: paramagnetic (Cu²⁺ has an unpaired electron)

cards.term: What are ferromagnetic substances?
cards.definition: Substances strongly magnetised in a field, strongly attracted, moving towards strong field

cards.term: What is a magnetic domain? Typical size and atoms?
cards.definition: A region where atomic moments align spontaneously (a quantum cooperative effect); ~1 mm, ~10¹¹ atoms

cards.term: What happens to domains in an external field B₀?
cards.definition: Domains rotate towards B₀, and those along B₀ grow, merging into one giant domain

cards.term: Why does an unmagnetised iron bar show no magnetisation?
cards.definition: Its domains point in random directions, so their moments cancel

cards.term: Are domains real? How are they seen?
cards.definition: Yes: sprinkle a liquid suspension of ferromagnetic powder and watch its motion under a microscope

cards.term: Hard vs soft ferromagnets?
cards.definition: Hard: magnetisation persists after the field is removed (permanent magnets). Soft: it disappears (electromagnet cores)

cards.term: Examples of hard and soft ferromagnetic materials?
cards.definition: Hard: Alnico (Fe, Al, Ni, Co, Cu), lodestone. Soft: soft iron

cards.term: Use of hard ferromagnets named by NCERT?
cards.definition: Permanent magnets, e.g. a compass needle

cards.text: Ferromagnetic elements: {{c1::iron, cobalt, nickel, gadolinium}}; their μᵣ is {{c2::> 1000}}.

cards.term: Effect of heating a ferromagnet?
cards.definition: Domains disintegrate and it becomes paramagnetic at high enough temperature; the loss of magnetisation is gradual

cards.term: Teacher addition: Curie temperature? Susceptibility above it?
cards.definition: T_C: temperature above which a ferromagnet turns paramagnetic; above it \( \chi = \dfrac{C}{T - T_C} \) (Curie–Weiss). Iron ≈ 1043 K

cards.term: Intuition: why do soft iron cores make strong electromagnets?
cards.definition: Huge μᵣ: domains line up with H and add μ₀M ≫ μ₀H; being soft, they switch off when the current stops

cards.term: Magnetic materials at a glance
cards.definition: Dia (χ<0), para (small +), ferro (≫1), superconductor (−1)

advancedHtml.backHtml:
Classification

Fill each class.

Diamagneticχ < 0, repelled, Bi Cu water
Paramagneticχ small +, weakly attracted, Al O₂
Ferromagneticχ ≫ 1, domains, Fe Co Ni
Superconductorχ = −1, perfect diamagnet

Only ferro- has domains; only para- follows χ ∝ 1/T

cards.term: Points to ponder: what does the compass teach about science and engineering?
cards.definition: Magnets were used for ~2000 years before magnetism was understood (after 1800) — understanding is not a precondition for applications

cards.term: Consequence of the non-existence of magnetic monopoles?
cards.definition: Magnetic field lines are continuous closed loops

cards.term: Typical χ of diamagnetic vs paramagnetic materials?
cards.definition: ≈ −10⁻⁵ vs +10⁻⁵ — a tiny difference, radically different behaviour

cards.term: Other magnetic classes beyond dia-, para- and ferro-?
cards.definition: Ferrimagnetic, antiferromagnetic, spin glass, …

cards.term: Dimensions of μ₀ and of B?
cards.definition: μ₀: [MLT⁻²A⁻²]; B: [MT⁻²A⁻¹]

cards.term: Correction: NCERT’s table gives the magnetic moment’s dimensions as [L⁻²A]. Right?
cards.definition: Typo: m = IA, so [L²A] (unit A m²)

cards.term: Correction: the Gauss box says he built the first electric telegraph with “Wilhelm Welser”. Who?
cards.definition: Wilhelm Weber (Gauss–Weber telegraph, Göttingen, 1833); the SI unit of flux is named after him

cards.term: Magnetic flux: unit, dimensions?
cards.definition: Weber (Wb = T m²); [ML²T⁻²A⁻¹]

cards.term: Note: are Earth’s magnetism and hysteresis in this chapter now?
cards.definition: No: they were removed in the rationalised NCERT, but some state boards and older papers still ask them

cards.term: Exercise 5.1: bar magnet at 30° to B = 0.25 T feels τ = 4.5 × 10⁻² J. m?
cards.definition: m = τ/(B sin 30°) = 0.36 J/T

cards.term: Exercise 5.2: m = 0.32 J/T in B = 0.15 T. Stable and unstable orientations and energies?
cards.definition: Stable: m ∥ B, U = −mB = −4.8 × 10⁻² J. Unstable: m antiparallel, U = +4.8 × 10⁻² J

cards.term: Exercise 5.3: 800 turns, A = 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ m², 3.0 A. In what sense is it a bar magnet? m?
cards.definition: Same field pattern and it aligns with an external field, with m along the axis (right-hand rule); m = NIA = 0.60 J/T

cards.term: Exercise 5.4: that solenoid at 30° to a horizontal B = 0.25 T. Torque?
cards.definition: τ = mB sin 30° = 0.6 × 0.25 × 0.5 = 7.5 × 10⁻² N m

cards.term: Correction: NCERT Exercise 5.4 refers to “the solenoid in Exercise 5.5”. Which one?
cards.definition: Exercise 5.3 (m = 0.60 J/T); 5.5 is about a bar magnet

cards.term: Work to rotate a bar magnet (Exercise 5.5)
cards.definition: W = 0.33 J and 0.66 J; τ = 0.33 N m and 0

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Exercise 5.5 · turning a magnet

Find the missing step.

m = 1.5 J/T aligned with B = 0.22 T. Work to turn it (i) normal to B, (ii) opposite to B; torque in each case?
  1. W = mB(cos θ₁ − cos θ₂), with θ₁ = 0
  2. (i) θ₂ = 90°: W = mB = 0.33 J
  3. ?
  4. τ = mB sin θ: (i) 0.33 N m, (ii) 0 (unstable equilibrium)
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Exercise 5.5 · turning a magnet

Find the missing step.

m = 1.5 J/T aligned with B = 0.22 T. Work to turn it (i) normal to B, (ii) opposite to B; torque in each case?
  1. W = mB(cos θ₁ − cos θ₂), with θ₁ = 0
  2. (i) θ₂ = 90°: W = mB = 0.33 J
  3. (ii) θ₂ = 180°: W = 2mB = 0.66 J
  4. τ = mB sin θ: (i) 0.33 N m, (ii) 0 (unstable equilibrium)

cards.term: Exercise 5.6: 2000 turns, A = 1.6 × 10⁻⁴ m², 4.0 A; B = 7.5 × 10⁻² T at 30° to the axis. m, force, torque?
cards.definition: m = 1.28 A m²; force 0 (uniform B); τ = mB sin 30° = 4.8 × 10⁻² N m

cards.term: Exercise 5.7: m = 0.48 J/T. B at 10 cm on the axis and on the equator?
cards.definition: Axis: 10⁻⁷ × 2 × 0.48/10⁻³ = 0.96 G (9.6 × 10⁻⁵ T) along S → N. Equator: 0.48 G, N → S (opposite to m)

cards.term: Chapter 5 formula sheet
cards.definition: Torque on dipole: τ = m × B; Energy of dipole: U = −m·B; Axial field: μ₀2m/4πr³; Equatorial field: −μ₀m/4πr³; Gauss’s law: ∮B·dS = 0; Magnetisation: M = m_net/V; B from H, M: B = μ₀(H + M); Susceptibility: χ = M/H; Permeability: μ = μ₀(1 + χ)
